name: Mustard plaster

card.summary: A traditional warming poultice of ground mustard seed that is applied to the skin as a counterirritant, used in folk and wellness circles for aches and congestion and occasionally discussed for circulation and skin.
card.note: Can cause first-degree burns, blistering and contact dermatitis if left on too long.

quick.overview:
A mustard plaster is a poultice made from powdered mustard seed, usually mixed with flour and water, spread inside a protective cloth dressing and placed on the body. It was part of conventional medicine in the 19th century and survives as a home remedy.

Its link to appearance is indirect and mostly claimed: it is used for muscle aches and soreness, which proponents connect to being able to keep training and recover, and as a warming skin treatment in some folk traditions. The research that exists concerns pain relief, not appearance.
quick.how: Traditionally the paste is wrapped in cloth rather than touching skin directly, applied for a limited time, and removed if the skin burns or stings. Users apply it over sore muscles, joints or the chest. Reports describe it being warming within minutes.
quick.risks: The main documented harms are skin redness, blisters, first-degree burns and phytocontact dermatitis from prolonged contact, and case reports include burns that resembled injuries. Children and people with sensitive skin or open wounds are at higher risk, and pediatric guidance sources do not recommend it for cough.

lead: A mustard plaster, historically also called a sinapism, is a poultice of mustard seed powder placed in a protective dressing and applied to the body to warm tissue and relieve chronic aches and pains.[1] It was once sold ready-made in pharmacies and used in conventional medical care, then declined in the twentieth century and is now mainly a home remedy.[1]

For appearance, the entry is a fringe one. Proponents use it for muscle and joint soreness, and the chain is that less soreness allows more consistent training and recovery. Some folk traditions also use warming mustard applications on the skin. The active irritant is allyl isothiocyanate, released when mustard seed is moistened.[2]
Research is limited to a small number of pain studies in older adults with knee osteoarthritis.[3][4]

chain: Warming counterirritant applied to a sore area
angle.text: Users apply it to aching muscles or joints for warmth and comfort. Any effect on physique runs through staying comfortable enough to keep training, not through changing the skin.

infobox: Ground mustard seed (Brassica or Sinapis species)

paras: The plaster combines mustard powder with flour and water to make a paste that is spread on a cloth, which keeps the paste from touching skin directly.[2] Black, brown and white mustard seed have all been used, and vinegar is sometimes substituted for water.[2]

Mustard has been used medicinally since antiquity, and writers from Hippocrates to Dioscorides are cited for mustard packs and plasters for aches and chest complaints.[2] Nicholas Culpeper's 1653 herbal described plasters that drew blisters.[2] A 1868 journal item and a 1971 article titled 'Bring back the mustard plaster' reflect its place in medical practice and later nostalgia.[5][6] Wikipedia notes a 1863 British Medical Journal report using the older term sinapism, and that the hymn writer Fanny Crosby was possibly blinded in infancy by mustard plasters.[1]

A 2024 one-group pretest-posttest study of 60 older adults with knee osteoarthritis applied a mustard plaster for 15 minutes daily over seven days and reported reductions in pain and improved function on the WOMAC scale.[3] A further study examined mustard plaster and knee pain perception in older people with osteoarthritis.[4] These studies lacked a comparison group in the first case, and no trial has examined appearance outcomes.

Left on too long it can cause first-degree burns, and its vapors may cause nausea.[1] A case report described phytocontact dermatitis from mustard seed that mimicked a burn injury,[7] and a German report described toxic dermatitis and phototoxic reactions after a mustard plaster was combined with bergamot oil.[8] Allyl isothiocyanate can cause redness, burns and nerve damage, and risks are higher in young children.[2]

timeline.event: Crew's Mustard Plaster appears in the Buffalo Medical and Surgical Journal.[5]
'Bring back the mustard plaster' published in Minnesota Medicine.[6]
